title: Negative Caching of DNS Queries
subtitle: How a resolver remembers that a name or record does not exist, and for how long.
summary: When a DNS lookup fails because the name or record type does not exist, a resolver can remember that fact instead of asking again. RFC 2308 defines how: the authoritative server attaches the zone's SOA record to the negative answer, and the SOA supplies the time to live. It also redefines the SOA MINIMUM field to mean exactly that, and makes negative caching a normal part of any caching resolver.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2308 lets DNS resolvers (the programs that look up names) remember that a name or record type does not exist, instead of asking again. The authoritative server attaches the zone's SOA record to the negative answer, and that record supplies how long the answer may be kept. It makes this caching a normal part of every caching resolver.

tldr.problem: A resolver that asked for a name or record that does not exist would ask again every time, and the original DNS rules gave no way to hand a cached "no" to other resolvers.
tldr.mechanism: The authoritative server puts the zone's SOA record in the authority section of every negative answer. Its TTL is the smaller of the SOA MINIMUM field and the SOA's own TTL, and caches count it down.
tldr.outcome: Negative answers are cached, counted down and passed along like positive ones, so the SOA MINIMUM field now controls how long a "no" lives.

today: Every mainstream caching resolver stores NXDOMAIN and NODATA answers, and zone operators still tune the last field of the SOA record to control how long a mistaken or newly created name stays "missing". The mechanism has been refined rather than replaced. RFC 4035 and its companions swapped the NXT record for NSEC, RFC 8020 says an NXDOMAIN for a name covers everything beneath it, and RFC 9520 adds caching of resolution failures.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The DNS lets a resolver cache the answers it receives so it need not ask again. RFC 1034 described caching of negative answers too, but it had what the abstract calls "a fundamental flaw": it did not let a name server hand those cached negative answers to other resolvers, which greatly reduced their usefulness. RFC 2308 replaces RFC 1034 section 4.3.4 and fixes that.

The RFC defines negative caching as "the storage of knowledge that something does not exist, cannot or does not give an answer." Its case for the feature is traffic: it reduces response time for negative answers and the number of messages between resolvers and name servers, and "a large proportion of DNS traffic on the Internet could be eliminated" if all resolvers did it. So negative caching "should no longer be seen as an optional part of a DNS resolver."

The RFC is written against the 1997 DNSSEC design, so it talks about NXT and SIG records. Those were later replaced by NSEC and RRSIG, but the caching rules are the same.
sections.plainLanguage: Negative caching means storing the fact that something does not exist or has no answer. The earlier DNS specification allowed it but did not let a name server pass cached negative answers on to other resolvers, which limited its use. This RFC fixes that. It argues that negative caching cuts response time and DNS traffic, so it should no longer be optional.

sections.title: What counts as a negative response
sections.content:
The RFC defines two main kinds. A name error, written NXDOMAIN, is the "Name Error" RCODE: the domain in the QNAME does not exist at all. NODATA is a pseudo-RCODE: the name exists for the class, but has no records of the requested type. A NODATA answer has RCODE NOERROR and nothing relevant in the answer section, so a resolver has to infer it from the contents.

The QNAME is the query name, unless it resolves through a CNAME chain, in which case it is the data of the last CNAME. That matters because an answer can carry CNAMEs and still be an NXDOMAIN about the name they point to.

The RFC shows four shapes of NXDOMAIN and three of NODATA, differing only in the authority section: Type 1 has an SOA and NS records, Type 2 has just an SOA, Type 3 has nothing, and NXDOMAIN Type 4 has only NS records. Some old resolvers mistook Type 1 for a referral, so authoritative servers are told to send Type 2, with an SOA and no NS records.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two main kinds of negative answer. NXDOMAIN means the name does not exist at all. NODATA means the name exists but has no records of the requested type. Authoritative servers are told to include only an SOA record, with no NS records, because some old resolvers mistook the NS records for a referral.

sections.title: Authoritative answers and the SOA minimum
sections.content:
An authoritative server "MUST include the SOA record of the zone in the authority section" when it reports NXDOMAIN or no data. This is "required so that the response may be cached," because a negative answer has no record of its own to carry a TTL. The SOA's TTL on the wire is "the minimum of the MINIMUM field of the SOA record and the TTL of the SOA itself." If the zone is signed, the SOA and the matching NXT and SIG records must be included too.

This forces a cleanup. The SOA minimum field had three meanings: the minimum TTL of all records in the zone, the default TTL for records with none, and the TTL for negative answers. The first, never used in practice, is deprecated. The second moves to a new master-file directive, $TTL <TTL> [comment], which sets the TTL for the records after it that do not give one. What is left is the new meaning of the field: the negative-answer TTL.

Negative answers from the zone are only as stale as this field allows. A server that publishes a new name must still wait out any cached "no" that resolvers stored before it appeared.
sections.plainLanguage: When an authoritative server reports NXDOMAIN or no data, it must include the zone's SOA record. A negative answer has no record of its own to carry a time to live (TTL), so the SOA supplies it. The SOA MINIMUM field now means exactly this: the TTL for negative answers. A new $TTL directive sets the default TTL for other records.

sections.title: Caching and replaying negative answers
sections.content:
The SOA record's TTL counts down like any cached answer, and "upon reaching zero (0) indicates the cached negative answer MUST NOT be used again." An NXDOMAIN is stored against <QNAME, QCLASS> and answers any later query for that name and class. A NODATA is stored against <QNAME, QTYPE, QCLASS> and answers only the same type. Negative responses without an SOA record "SHOULD NOT be cached," because without a TTL countdown a "no" could circulate forever between two servers configured as each other's forwarders.

When a server answers from its cache it "MUST add the cached SOA record" to the authority section, with the TTL decremented by the time stored, so the next resolver can time it out correctly. A cached NXT must be included too. Cached negative answers should also carry an implicit referral, NS records pointing toward an authoritative source.

A resolver should cap how long it keeps a negative answer: the protocol allows up to 68 years, the cap should not exceed the one for positive answers and should be tunable, "values of one to three hours have been found to work well," and values over a day "have been found to be problematic."
sections.plainLanguage: A cached negative answer counts down like any other and must not be used once it reaches zero. An NXDOMAIN applies to every query for that name. A NODATA applies only to the same record type. A resolver that answers from its cache must include the SOA with the reduced TTL, so the next resolver can expire it correctly. Keeping answers for one to three hours has worked well.

sections.title: Failures and dead servers
sections.content:
Section 7 covers negative signals that carry no SOA, and both are optional. A server failure (a misconfigured zone, or an upstream that could not be reached) may be cached, "MUST NOT" for longer than five minutes, and only against the tuple <query name, type, class, server IP address>.

A dead or unreachable server is one that has not answered an outstanding query within 120 seconds, or about which the transport layer gave an indication, such as ICMP host, net or port unreachable, or a TCP reset. A resolver may remember it, again for at most five minutes. The indication is tied to the same four-part tuple, unless the transport said the server does not exist, in which case it applies to every query to that IP address.

The RFC says there is no way to put a TTL in these responses, which is why the limit is fixed and short. It also warns to take care that there are no forwarding loops.
sections.plainLanguage: Two kinds of failure carry no SOA and may optionally be cached: a server failure, and a server that is dead or unreachable. A server counts as dead if it has not answered within 120 seconds or the transport layer reported an error. These may be remembered for at most five minutes, because no TTL can be attached to them.

sections.title: Security considerations
sections.content:
The RFC believes the document adds no significant threat beyond using DNS data in general, but it names one effect. With negative caching, "it might be possible to propagate a denial of service attack by spreading a NXDOMAIN message with a very high TTL." The RFC compares this to spreading a bad A record, and says the effect on the user is different: a broken A record feels like a broken network, while NXDOMAIN feels as if the server was turned off. Its example is an SMTP server that bounces a message at once on NXDOMAIN, where a bad A record would only have queued the mail.

For the attack to work, the bogus NXDOMAIN has to be injected into a parent server or a busy caching resolver, for example by using a CNAME that makes the parent query an attacker's server. Resolvers can defend by asking again for the final QNAME and ignoring any NS data in the responses. TTL sanity checking also helps, since the attacker must re-inject more often.

The RFC also points to DNS Security (RFC 2065), which can verify a negative response with NXT and SIG records.
sections.plainLanguage: Negative caching adds one risk. An attacker who spreads a false NXDOMAIN with a very high TTL could make a working name appear not to exist. This is worse than a bad address record, because the failure looks like a server that was turned off. Resolvers can defend by checking the final query name again and by sanity-checking TTLs. DNS Security can verify negative answers.

sections.title: History and what changed from RFC 1034
sections.content:
Section 8 lists the changes: negative caching in resolvers "is no-longer optional, if a resolver caches anything it must also cache negative answers"; non-authoritative negative answers may be cached; the SOA from the authority section must be cached; and a cached SOA must now be added to the response, which RFC 1034 had not allowed. The $TTL directive was added to the master file format.

Section 9 is a history marked "no part of the technical specification." Rob Austein recalls that around spring 1985 Paul Mockapetris suggested caching authoritative errors using the zone's SOA MINIMUM, and that his CHIVES resolver was, as far as he knew, the first to implement negative caching. The same ideas were re-invented in BIND. Anant Kumar's code in BIND 4.9.2 ALPHA (July 1993) used a ten-minute TTL, and the SOA-storing RETURNSOA option was turned off in April 1994, after complaints about old answers following a zone reload, and re-enabled by default in BIND 4.9.5-T1A in August 1996.
sections.plainLanguage: Compared with RFC 1034, negative caching is no longer optional: a resolver that caches anything must also cache negative answers. Non-authoritative negative answers may be cached, and a cached SOA must be added to responses. The $TTL directive was added to the master file format. The RFC also includes a history of how negative caching developed in early DNS software.

data.title: SOA with a 20-minute negative TTL
data.code:
$TTL 86400
$ORIGIN XX.EXAMPLE.
@  IN  SOA  NS1.XX.EXAMPLE. HOSTMATER.XX.EXAMPLE. (
           1997102000 ; serial
           1800       ; refresh (30 mins)
           900        ; retry (15 mins)
           604800     ; expire (7 days)
           1200 )     ; minimum (20 mins)
